background.authorship: The heading contains only לְדָוִד, conventionally ‘of David’; it does not contain the word ‘psalm’ or name an occasion. The preposition can express authorship, dedication or association, so ‘by David’, ‘for David’ and ‘belonging to the Davidic collection’ represent different understandings. Traditional Jewish and Christian interpretation commonly treats David as the speaker and author. Historical criticism distinguishes that attribution from independently established authorship: an otherwise unidentified poet could speak within a Davidic or royal tradition. Yale Bible Study describes the broader scholarly understanding of Davidic headings as evidence of the Psalms’ transmission and interpretation, rather than automatic proof of authorship. [Yale Bible Study](https://yalebiblestudy.org/courses/the-gospel-of-matthew/lessons/what-are-the-psalms-study-guide/)
background.form:
This is an individual lament or petition that turns into thanksgiving and communal intercession: verses 1–5 plead for hearing and judgment, verses 6–7 celebrate help, and verses 8–9 widen the focus. There is no alphabetic acrostic, Selah, tune name or instrumental instruction. The Hebrew accents mark recitation and phrasing; they do not prescribe modern 6/8 time. That requested meter fixes two main beats per bar, not six syllables per line.

Important links include hearing and silence in verses 1–2 and 6; the recurring phrase ‘voice of my supplications’ in verses 2 and 6, with ‘hear’ changing to ‘has heard’; the worshipper’s hands in verse 2, the enemies’ hands in verse 4 and God’s hands in verse 5; evil hearts in verse 3 and the trusting, rejoicing heart in verse 7; and the related sounds עֹז, ‘strength’, and מָעוֹז, ‘stronghold’, in verses 7–8. There is no marked recurring chorus. Adding one would be a musical arrangement decision.

Swete, The Old Testament in Greek according to the Septuagint, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1896), Psalms; transcribed from page images by the rahlfs1931-psalter project, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0. background.reception:
Rashi understands the ‘them’ in verse 8 as those who rely on God, identified with Israel, and connects the announced thanksgiving in verse 7 with what follows. This supports a continuous movement from personal gratitude to communal praise. [Rashi](https://www.chabad.org/library/bible_cdo/aid/16249/jewish/Chapter-28.htm) In Jewish practice, the ten Hebrew words of verse 9 are used to ascertain a minyan without counting people numerically; that use depends on the Hebrew wording, not an English word count. [Kitzur Shulchan Arukh 15:3](https://hebrewbible.app/en/resources/halakhah/Psalms.28.9)

Augustine reads the psalm as Christ’s voice in suffering and resurrection. His interpretation of renewed flesh depends on the Greek-derived reading in verse 7, which differs from the Masoretic rejoicing heart. That reception should remain distinguishable from the Hebrew wording. [Augustine](https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801028.htm) Verse 9 enters Christian worship through the Te Deum, where the Book of Common Prayer uses governing and lifting language. [Church of England](https://www.churchofengland.org/prayer-and-worship/worship-texts-and-resources/common-worship/common-material/canticles-main-1) Second Timothy 4:14 is identified by the NET notes as an allusion to verse 4’s repayment according to deeds; it is not an explicitly introduced quotation of Psalm 28. [NET note](https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=2Ti&chapter=4&tab=commentaries&verse=14)
background.setting:
The text depicts someone fearing death, seeking a hearing from God, distinguishing himself from deceitful evildoers, and praying toward a sanctuary. It ends with the anointed ruler and the people. It names no illness, battle, rebellion or historical event. A Davidic setting would place it around the tenth century BCE. A. F. Kirkpatrick reports the traditional association with David’s flight from Absalom: treacherous neighbors become conspirators, and the closing petition concerns a divided nation. He also considers an epidemic, because the speaker fears sharing the wicked’s death. These are reconstructions, not information supplied by the heading. [Kirkpatrick](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/psalms/28.htm)

A royal prayer used in sanctuary worship is another reconstruction, supported by the sanctuary in verse 2 and the anointed figure in verse 8; a living Judean king would suggest a setting before the monarchy ended in 586 BCE, without identifying a reign. The inner-sanctuary vocabulary fits temple worship but cannot by itself date the poem. Ellicott’s commentary proposes serious illness and regards verses 8–9 as a possible communal addition; that proposal supplies no secure date for either part. [Ellicott](https://truthaccordingtoscripture.com/commentaries/ebc/psalms-28.php)
background.themes: The opening danger is God’s apparent nonresponse: without a hearing, the speaker will resemble those descending to death. The prayer then asks that outwardly peaceful but inwardly malicious people receive the consequences of their actions. Their handiwork is contrasted with the divine handiwork they disregard. The turning point is the declaration that God has heard. Trust, help and joy replace threatened silence, and personal rescue becomes a basis for praying for the people. Rock, shield, stronghold and shepherd present complementary pictures of protection. The text leaves the precise experience behind its turn to thanksgiving unstated.

background.authorship: The heading contains only לְדָוִד, conventionally ‘of David’; it does not contain the word ‘psalm’ or name an occasion. The preposition can express authorship, dedication or association, so ‘by David’, ‘for David’ and ‘belonging to the Davidic collection’ represent different understandings. Traditional Jewish and Christian interpretation commonly treats David as the speaker and author. Historical criticism distinguishes that attribution from independently established authorship: an otherwise unidentified poet could speak within a Davidic or royal tradition. Yale Bible Study describes the broader scholarly understanding of Davidic headings as evidence of the Psalms’ transmission and interpretation, rather than automatic proof of authorship. [Yale Bible Study](https://yalebiblestudy.org/courses/the-gospel-of-matthew/lessons/what-are-the-psalms-study-guide/)
background.form:
This is an individual lament or petition that turns into thanksgiving and communal intercession: verses 1–5 plead for hearing and judgment, verses 6–7 celebrate help, and verses 8–9 widen the focus. There is no alphabetic acrostic, Selah, tune name or instrumental instruction. The Hebrew accents mark recitation and phrasing; they do not prescribe modern 6/8 time. That requested meter fixes two main beats per bar, not six syllables per line.

Important links include hearing and silence in verses 1–2 and 6; the recurring phrase ‘voice of my supplications’ in verses 2 and 6, with ‘hear’ changing to ‘has heard’; the worshipper’s hands in verse 2, the enemies’ hands in verse 4 and God’s hands in verse 5; evil hearts in verse 3 and the trusting, rejoicing heart in verse 7; and the related sounds עֹז, ‘strength’, and מָעוֹז, ‘stronghold’, in verses 7–8. There is no marked recurring chorus. Adding one would be a musical arrangement decision.

Greek comparisons below refer specifically to the supplied Swete 1896 text, Greek Psalm 27 corresponding to Masoretic Psalm 28, with the supplied verse mapping still proposed. Provenance: H. B. Swete, The Old Testament in Greek according to the Septuagint, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1896), Psalms; transcribed from page images by the rahlfs1931-psalter project, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0. Source IDs: lxx, swete1896. Source version: swete1896:r0001:edda9c613905b0a0161deb0fe7fd5a0a79beda5d0f83fe13cf354f514d3f957e. This briefing identifies alternatives without adopting a Greek variant or generating verse translation candidates.
background.reception:
Rashi understands the ‘them’ in verse 8 as those who rely on God, identified with Israel, and connects the announced thanksgiving in verse 7 with what follows. This supports a continuous movement from personal gratitude to communal praise. [Rashi](https://www.chabad.org/library/bible_cdo/aid/16249/jewish/Chapter-28.htm) In Jewish practice, the ten Hebrew words of verse 9 are used to ascertain a minyan without counting people numerically; that use depends on the Hebrew wording, not an English word count. [Kitzur Shulchan Arukh 15:3](https://hebrewbible.app/en/resources/halakhah/Psalms.28.9)

Augustine reads the psalm as Christ’s voice in suffering and resurrection. His interpretation of renewed flesh depends on the Greek-derived reading in verse 7, which differs from the Masoretic rejoicing heart. That reception should remain distinguishable from the Hebrew wording. [Augustine](https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801028.htm) Verse 9 enters Christian worship through the Te Deum, where the Book of Common Prayer uses governing and lifting language. [Church of England](https://www.churchofengland.org/prayer-and-worship/worship-texts-and-resources/common-worship/common-material/canticles-main-1) Second Timothy 4:14 is identified by the NET notes as an allusion to verse 4’s repayment according to deeds; it is not an explicitly introduced quotation of Psalm 28. [NET note](https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=2Ti&chapter=4&tab=commentaries&verse=14)
background.setting:
The text depicts someone fearing death, seeking a hearing from God, distinguishing himself from deceitful evildoers, and praying toward a sanctuary. It ends with the anointed ruler and the people. It names no illness, battle, rebellion or historical event. A Davidic setting would place it around the tenth century BCE. A. F. Kirkpatrick reports the traditional association with David’s flight from Absalom: treacherous neighbors become conspirators, and the closing petition concerns a divided nation. He also considers an epidemic, because the speaker fears sharing the wicked’s death. These are reconstructions, not information supplied by the heading. [Kirkpatrick](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/psalms/28.htm)

A royal prayer used in sanctuary worship is another reconstruction, supported by the sanctuary in verse 2 and the anointed figure in verse 8; a living Judean king would suggest a setting before the monarchy ended in 586 BCE, without identifying a reign. The inner-sanctuary vocabulary fits temple worship but cannot by itself date the poem. Ellicott’s commentary proposes serious illness and regards verses 8–9 as a possible communal addition; that proposal supplies no secure date for either part. [Ellicott](https://truthaccordingtoscripture.com/commentaries/ebc/psalms-28.php)
background.themes: The opening danger is God’s apparent nonresponse: without a hearing, the speaker will resemble those descending to death. The prayer then asks that outwardly peaceful but inwardly malicious people receive the consequences of their actions. Their handiwork is contrasted with the divine handiwork they disregard. The turning point is the declaration that God has heard. Trust, help and joy replace threatened silence, and personal rescue becomes a basis for praying for the people. Rock, shield, stronghold and shepherd present complementary pictures of protection. The text leaves the precise experience behind its turn to thanksgiving unstated.

[UBS translation discussion](https://tips.translation.bible/tip_verse/ps-287/)

options.choice: Make song the means of thanksgiving.
options.effect: Keeps the explicit musical reference and its relevance to a sung setting; does not express the Greek emphasis on willingness.
options.held_by: Masoretic text; KJV, ASV and WEB.

options.choice: Express willing or freely offered thanksgiving.
options.effect: Makes voluntary devotion explicit; removes the Hebrew reference to a song.
options.held_by: Swete 1896, Greek Psalm 27:7; Augustine’s Greek-derived exposition.

options.choice: Express thanksgiving with the whole body and identify the alternative reading.
options.effect: Gives the thanksgiving an embodied character; requires a textual departure beyond the supplied Hebrew and Greek readings.
options.held_by: New English Bible, as documented by Bratcher and Reyburn.

questions.question: What should express the manner of the closing thanksgiving in verse 7?

questions.background: The Masoretic לָמוֹ means ‘to them’, but its antecedent is not immediately expressed. Swete, Greek Psalm 27:8, explicitly has τοῦ λαοῦ αὐτοῦ, ‘of his people’. NET discusses a corresponding Hebrew reading לְעַמּוֹ; Rashi instead explains the received pronoun as those who rely on God. [NET textual note](https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Psa+28%3A8%2C9)

options.choice: Keep ‘their strength’ and leave the group implicit.
options.effect: Preserves the received wording and its openness; listeners must infer the referent.
options.held_by: Masoretic text; KJV, ASV and WEB; Rashi explains the pronoun without replacing it.

options.choice: Name ‘his people’, identifying the Greek or alternative Hebrew basis.
options.effect: Makes the communal transition immediately clear; adopts wording beyond the supplied Masoretic text.
options.held_by: Swete 1896, Greek Psalm 27:8; NET and RSV.

questions.question: Should verse 8 retain ‘their’ or explicitly name God’s people?
questions.topic: Their strength or the people’s strength

questions.background: מְשִׁיחוֹ is singular, ‘his anointed one’. Swete’s τοῦ χριστοῦ αὐτοῦ is the corresponding Greek expression, not automatically the English proper name ‘Christ’. NET identifies the Davidic king; a collective interpretation is reported in the New Jerusalem Bible’s note; Augustine reads the figure christologically. [UBS discussion](https://tips.translation.bible/story/translation-commentary-on-psalm-288/)

options.choice: Keep ‘his anointed’ without further identification.
options.effect: Preserves the title’s historical and later interpretive possibilities; may leave unfamiliar listeners uncertain.
options.held_by: KJV, ASV and WEB.

options.choice: Identify the anointed figure as God’s chosen or anointed king.
options.effect: Clarifies the likely royal reference; narrows an expression that the Hebrew leaves as a title.
options.held_by: NET; the royal interpretation explained by Bratcher and Reyburn.

options.choice: Present the anointed figure collectively as God’s people.
options.effect: Strengthens the parallel with the people; interprets a singular title corporately.
options.held_by: The possibility noted in the New Jerusalem Bible, as reported by Bratcher and Reyburn.

options.choice: Use an explicitly messianic designation and identify the Christian interpretive basis.
options.effect: Makes Christian reception audible; places a particular theological identification in the main wording.
options.held_by: Augustine’s christological reading.

questions.question: How explicitly should ‘his anointed’ identify a king, a community or the Messiah?

questions.background: The Hebrew יֶהֶרְסֵם וְלֹא יִבְנֵם uses third-person forms that translators take as prediction or as a wish in this prayer context. Swete, Greek Psalm 27:5, instead uses second-person future forms: καθελεῖς and οἰκοδομήσεις. Mood and grammatical person are separate decisions. [UBS discussion](https://tips.translation.bible/story/translation-commentary-on-psalm-285/)

options.choice: Use a third-person prediction: God will tear down and will not rebuild.
options.effect: Marks a movement toward certainty before verse 6; ends the petition earlier.
options.held_by: KJV, ASV, WEB and RSV.

options.choice: Continue with a third-person wish or appeal: may God tear down and not rebuild.
options.effect: Keeps verse 5 within the prayer for judgment; postpones the clear declaration of assurance.
options.held_by: Revised English Bible; JPS translation displayed by Sefaria.

options.choice: Follow Swete’s direct-address future: you will tear down and will not rebuild.
options.effect: Combines certainty with continued address to God; changes the grammatical person of the supplied Hebrew.
options.held_by: Swete 1896, Greek Psalm 27:5.

questions.question: Should the ending of verse 5 continue the petition or declare what God will do, and should it address God directly?

questions.background: אֶקְרָא in verse 1 can be presented as ‘I call’ or ‘I will call’; Swete has the past ἐκέκραξα. Verses 6–7 use completed-action forms for hearing, trusting and receiving help, followed by rejoicing and a prospective expression of thanks. These forms do not alone establish whether rescue has already occurred or is confidently anticipated. Kirkpatrick discusses both interpretations. [Kirkpatrick](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/psalms/28.htm)

options.choice: Present the opening as current prayer and the help and rejoicing as events already experienced.
options.effect: Creates a clear narrative of prayer answered; can make the transition sound like an elapsed interval.
options.held_by: WEB’s present opening; the past-tense sequence in the Judaica Press translation displayed by Chabad.

options.choice: Use future or ongoing calling, completed trust, and present help and joy.
options.effect: Emphasizes a present state of confidence grounded in trust; leaves the chronology less explicit.
options.held_by: KJV and ASV use this mixture of times.

options.choice: Use Swete’s past opening and retrospective help, followed by promised thanksgiving.
options.effect: Makes the opening call retrospective; departs from a straightforward present rendering of the Hebrew opening.
options.held_by: Swete 1896, Greek Psalm 27:1, 6–7.

questions.question: How should English distinguish present prayer, completed help and continuing trust or joy?
questions.topic: Time and the turn to thanksgiving

questions.background: The requested time signature is already decided. It does not determine melody, syllable count, rhyme or stanza length. Verse 4’s repeated requests and the longer clauses in verses 1 and 7 create different musical demands from verse 6’s brief thanksgiving.

options.choice: Allow varying numbers of bars, pickups and sustained notes while retaining the clauses and repeated wording.
options.effect: Keeps more of the source’s rhetoric and imagery; requires a less uniform melody or phrase structure.
options.held_by: Editorial option for this project, compatible with the clause-preserving approaches of KJV, ASV and WEB; those versions do not themselves prescribe 6/8.

options.choice: Use a recurring stanza pattern and declare any compressed repetitions or explanatory additions.
options.effect: Supports a readily repeated tune; makes the choice of what to shorten or expand more consequential.
options.held_by: Editorial option for this project; no Hebrew or Greek witness prescribes this arrangement.

questions.question: Within 6/8, should phrase lengths vary to preserve the parallel clauses, or should the text be compressed into a recurring stanza pattern?

questions.background: The heading belongs to verse 1 in the supplied numbering. ‘By David’ makes authorship explicit; ‘of David’ preserves a broader association. Adding ‘a psalm’ or ‘a song’ supplies a word absent from both the Hebrew heading and Swete’s Τοῦ Δαυείδ.

options.choice: Retain ‘Of David’ as an unsung heading.
options.effect: Keeps the attribution visible without forcing it into the prayer’s meter; leaves its precise relationship to David open.
options.held_by: The wording of KJV and ASV, with their supplied ‘A Psalm’ omitted; unsung placement is a performance decision.

options.choice: Use ‘By David’ as the heading.
options.effect: States the traditional authorship interpretation clearly; removes the broader ambiguity of the Hebrew preposition.
options.held_by: The supplied WEB.

options.choice: Sing the attribution, identifying any added words such as ‘a song’.
options.effect: Makes the heading part of the audible setting; needs musical space and may require an explicit expansion.
options.held_by: Editorial performance option for this project.

questions.question: How should לְדָוִד be worded, and should it be sung or retained as an unsung heading?

questions.background: The first-person voice gives way to statements about the people and anointed figure, then direct prayer for them. No speaker label marks a change. Rashi connects the thanksgiving with what follows, and the Traduction œcuménique de la Bible takes verses 8–9 as the song announced in verse 7. [UBS discussion](https://tips.translation.bible/story/translation-commentary-on-psalm-288/)

options.choice: Keep one continuous speaker without quotation marks or a new speaker label.
options.effect: Preserves the text’s lack of explicit staging; the communal widening must be heard through the words.
options.held_by: KJV, ASV and WEB leave the transition unmarked.

options.choice: Present verses 8–9 as the content of the song announced in verse 7.
options.effect: Makes the final section’s relation to the thanksgiving clear; adds an interpretive structural boundary.
options.held_by: Traduction œcuménique de la Bible; a related connection appears in Rashi.

options.choice: Assign the ending to a congregation or responding choir while identifying that assignment as arrangement.
options.effect: Makes the move from individual to community audible; introduces performers not specified in the source.
options.held_by: Editorial realization of the communal-ending interpretation discussed by Ellicott.

questions.question: Should the closing communal words remain the individual’s prayer, become the announced song, or be assigned to a responding group?

questions.background: The Hebrew צוּרִי explicitly supplies the rock metaphor. Swete, Greek Psalm 27:1, instead has ὁ θεός μου. This is a difference between witnesses, not evidence that Elohim occurs in the supplied Hebrew.

options.choice: Retain ‘my rock’.
options.effect: Preserves the first of the psalm’s protection images; requires listeners to understand the metaphor.
options.held_by: Masoretic text; KJV, ASV and WEB.

options.choice: Use ‘my God’ on the stated basis of Swete’s Greek.
options.effect: Preserves the Greek address and its reception; removes the Hebrew rock image.
options.held_by: Swete 1896, Greek Psalm 27:1; Augustine’s Greek-derived text.

questions.question: Should the opening address retain ‘my rock’ or follow the Greek ‘my God’?

questions.background: תֶּחֱרַשׁ can describe being deaf or keeping silent; תֶּחֱשֶׁה concerns silence or inactivity. Swete repeats παρασιωπήσῃς in both positions. The Hebrew therefore permits a distinction that the supplied Greek does not reproduce.

options.choice: Distinguish ‘do not be deaf’ from ‘if you are silent’.
options.effect: Links God’s hearing and answering while preserving two images; uses potentially unfamiliar language about divine deafness.
options.held_by: ASV and WEB.

options.choice: Use silence language in both clauses.
options.effect: Creates a clear verbal repetition suited to music; reduces the distinction between hearing and responding.
options.held_by: KJV; Swete 1896, Greek Psalm 27:1.

questions.question: Should the two opening verbs distinguish not hearing from not answering, or repeat the image of silence?

questions.background: וְנִמְשַׁלְתִּי expresses becoming like others, not necessarily being literally dragged into their company. יוֹרְדֵי בוֹר depicts those descending to the pit, conventionally the dying or dead. The phrase does not itself specify hell as a place of punishment. [Kirkpatrick](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/psalms/28.htm)

options.choice: Keep the comparison and the descent-to-the-pit image.
options.effect: Retains the source’s spatial poetry and ambiguity between dying and dead; may need explanation outside the sung text.
options.held_by: KJV, ASV, WEB and Swete 1896, Greek Psalm 27:1.

options.choice: Make death or the grave explicit while preserving the comparison.
options.effect: Makes the danger immediately intelligible; resolves part of the original image’s openness.
options.held_by: The interpretation explained by Kirkpatrick.

questions.question: Should the threatened fate remain an image of descent to the pit or be explained as death?
questions.topic: The pit and the feared consequence

questions.background: דְּבִיר קָדְשֶׁךָ points to the holy inner sanctuary. Swete, Greek Psalm 27:2, has ναὸν ἅγιόν σου, a holy temple or sanctuary without explicitly reproducing ‘inner’. The traditional English ‘oracle’ is now liable to suggest a spoken revelation rather than a room.

options.choice: Name the inner sanctuary or Most Holy Place.
options.effect: Preserves the architectural specificity; introduces terminology that may be harder to fit into a short phrase.
options.held_by: WEB uses ‘Most Holy Place’; the Hebrew-based interpretation in modern Jewish translations.

options.choice: Use the broader ‘holy temple’ or ‘holy sanctuary’, identifying the Greek basis where adopted.
options.effect: Gives a familiar, compact worship setting; loses the Hebrew emphasis on the innermost room.
options.held_by: Swete 1896, Greek Psalm 27:2.

options.choice: Retain ‘holy oracle’ as traditional sanctuary language.
options.effect: Preserves a recognizable older English phrasing; risks being heard as an utterance or divination.
options.held_by: KJV and ASV.

questions.question: How specifically should the destination of the raised hands be named?

questions.background: קוֹל תַּחֲנוּנַי recurs in both verses; the hearing verb changes from an imperative to a completed form. תַּחֲנוּנִים expresses earnest entreaties, often for favor or mercy. Swete also repeats the corresponding phrase, using a singular noun for supplication.

options.choice: Keep ‘voice’ and the same noun for supplications, petitions or pleading in both places.
options.effect: Preserves the audible request-and-answer link; retains a phrase longer than a simple ‘hear my prayer’.
options.held_by: KJV and ASV use ‘voice of my supplications’; WEB uses ‘voice of my petitions’.

options.choice: Use the same shorter expression for a plea or prayer in both places.
options.effect: Fits shorter musical phrases and communicates the appeal directly; compresses ‘voice’ and the Hebrew plural.
options.held_by: The JPS rendering displayed by Sefaria uses a compact plea-for-mercy expression. [Sefaria](https://www.sefaria.org/Psalms.28?with=Rashi)

questions.question: How should the repeated expression for pleading be worded so that the answer recalls the request?

questions.background: תִּמְשְׁכֵנִי normally evokes drawing or dragging the speaker along. Some translations make the implied classification explicit: the speaker asks not to share the wicked’s fate. The JPS text displayed by Sefaria offers a counting interpretation and notes dragging as an alternative. [Sefaria](https://www.sefaria.org/Psalms.28?with=Rashi)

options.choice: Keep ‘draw’ or ‘drag me away’ with the wicked.
options.effect: Preserves the forceful action and vulnerability; leaves the implied judgment to context.
options.held_by: KJV, ASV and WEB; Rashi retains the drawing image.

options.choice: Express not being counted or treated with the wicked.
options.effect: Clarifies the plea against sharing their status or fate; replaces a concrete action with its interpreted meaning.
options.held_by: The JPS translation displayed by Sefaria.

questions.question: Should the opening request emphasize physical removal or being treated as belonging with the wicked?
questions.topic: Being dragged away or counted with evildoers

questions.background: Swete, Greek Psalm 27:3, includes τὴν ψυχήν μου, ‘my soul/life’, and a second prohibition, μὴ συναπολέσῃς με, asking not to be destroyed together with evildoers. Neither has a separate equivalent in the supplied Hebrew.

options.choice: Follow the Hebrew’s single request with its two descriptions of evildoers.
options.effect: Keeps the shorter construction and leaves the ultimate fate implicit; does not reproduce the fuller Greek petition.
options.held_by: Masoretic text; KJV, ASV and WEB.

options.choice: Include the Greek’s reference to the speaker’s life and explicit plea against shared destruction.
options.effect: Makes the danger explicit and strengthens the parallel petitions; adds material absent from the supplied Hebrew and lengthens the setting.
options.held_by: Swete 1896, Greek Psalm 27:3.

questions.question: Should verse 3 retain the shorter Hebrew request or include the Greek’s explicit soul and destruction clauses?

questions.background: דֹּבְרֵי שָׁלוֹם concerns speech of peace or goodwill with neighbors; רָעָה בִּלְבָבָם places evil in their heart. The Hebrew need not describe a formal peace agreement. ‘Heart’ includes intention and thought, not only feeling.

options.choice: Keep peace on their lips or in their speech and evil in their hearts.
options.effect: Preserves the vocabulary and the contrast with verse 7’s heart; leaves the precise kind of deception unstated.
options.held_by: KJV, ASV and WEB; Swete retains peace and hearts.

options.choice: Express professed goodwill toward neighbors and inward malice.
options.effect: Makes the social hypocrisy clear in contemporary English; reduces the literal peace-and-heart imagery.
options.held_by: The JPS translation displayed by Sefaria.

questions.question: Should the contrast retain ‘peace’ and ‘heart’, or explain them as friendly speech and concealed malice?

questions.background: תֶּן ... תֵּן ... הָשֵׁב gives two requests to give and one to return. The standard of recompense is repeatedly the enemies’ own deeds. גְּמוּלָם can be expressed as their recompense or what they deserve; English ‘reward’ can misleadingly sound favorable.

options.choice: Retain the repeated commands and the repeated comparison with their deeds.
options.effect: Keeps the prayer’s insistence and proportional judgment; requires musical space for deliberate repetition.
options.held_by: KJV, ASV and WEB; Swete, Greek Psalm 27:4, likewise preserves repeated imperatives.

options.choice: Condense the parallel requests into a shorter plea for repayment according to their deeds, declaring the compression.
options.effect: Fits a more regular stanza; reduces the cumulative rhetorical pressure.
options.held_by: Editorial metrical option for this project, rather than a different ancient reading.

questions.question: How should the repeated requests for repayment retain their force within the meter?

questions.background: לֹא יָבִינוּ אֶל can describe failure to understand or attend to something. In this context, English versions differ over whether to foreground perception or culpable disregard. Swete, Greek Psalm 27:5, uses οὐ συνῆκαν, a past expression of not understanding. [UBS discussion](https://tips.translation.bible/story/translation-commentary-on-psalm-285/)

options.choice: Describe their failure to consider or pay attention to God’s works.
options.effect: Preserves room for both perception and moral neglect; may sound less explicit about their hostility.
options.held_by: KJV and ASV use ‘regard not’; NASB also uses ‘regard’.

options.choice: Describe their lack of respect for God’s works.
options.effect: Makes the ethical failure plain; interprets the cognitive verb as an attitude.
options.held_by: The supplied WEB.

options.choice: Describe their failure to understand, using past time if following Swete.
options.effect: Foregrounds comprehension and the Greek verbal perspective; may sound like ignorance unless the surrounding context supplies culpability.
options.held_by: Swete 1896, Greek Psalm 27:5.

questions.question: Should the enemies’ failure be described as lack of understanding, lack of attention or lack of respect?
questions.topic: Ignoring or failing to understand God’s works

questions.background: The speaker raises hands; the wicked perform the work of their hands; they ignore the work of God’s hands. Verse 5 then pictures their destruction as demolition without rebuilding. These links can disappear if each occurrence is independently paraphrased.

options.choice: Repeat ‘hands’ and related work vocabulary, and retain tearing down versus rebuilding.
options.effect: Keeps the moral contrast and architectural ending audible; retains several physical metaphors for divine action.
options.held_by: ASV and WEB closely preserve these links.

options.choice: Use more abstract action language where needed, while retaining the contrast between human deeds and God’s deeds.
options.effect: Can make short lyric phrases clearer; weakens the network of hands and construction images.
options.held_by: KJV partly does this with ‘destroy’ in verse 5; broader compression is an editorial option.

questions.question: How much of the repeated hands, work and building imagery should remain explicit?

questions.background: עֻזִּי וּמָגִנִּי gives ‘my strength and my shield’. Some interpreters take the pair together as a strong shield or mighty protector. Swete, Greek Psalm 27:7, has βοηθός and ὑπερασπιστής, helper and defender. [UBS discussion](https://tips.translation.bible/tip_verse/ps-287/)

options.choice: Keep ‘my strength and my shield’ as two expressions.
options.effect: Preserves both Hebrew terms and the repeated strength language in verse 8; keeps a concrete martial image.
options.held_by: KJV, ASV and WEB.

options.choice: Combine the pair as a strong shield or mighty protector.
options.effect: Produces a compact single image; interprets the conjunction as joining words that express one idea.
options.held_by: Mitchell Dahood; Biblia Dios Habla Hoy, as reported by Bratcher and Reyburn.

options.choice: Use helper and defender on the basis of Swete’s Greek.
options.effect: Emphasizes personal assistance and protection; removes the explicit Hebrew strength-and-shield pair.
options.held_by: Swete 1896, Greek Psalm 27:7.

questions.question: Should verse 7 retain two protection expressions, combine them, or follow the Greek personal descriptions?

questions.background: אֲהוֹדֶנּוּ can express thankful acknowledgment or praise. The immediate context of received help favors thanksgiving as a natural sense, while public praise remains part of the expression’s range. Swete uses ἐξομολογήσομαι, which likewise need not mean confession of sins here.

options.choice: Use a verb of thanking.
options.effect: Connects the response directly with received help; foregrounds gratitude over broader praise.
options.held_by: WEB; the Judaica Press translation displayed by Chabad.

options.choice: Use a verb of praising.
options.effect: Gives a familiar worship expression with broad scope; makes the specific thanksgiving less explicit.
options.held_by: KJV and ASV.

questions.question: Should the final verb emphasize giving thanks or offering praise?

questions.background: מָעוֹז יְשׁוּעוֹת combines a refuge or stronghold with a plural noun for salvations or deliverances. English can retain the unusual plurality, use a collective ‘salvation’, or turn the phrase into protective action. Swete, Greek Psalm 27:8, uses a defender expression and also retains a plural form.

options.choice: Retain a stronghold or refuge of salvation, using ‘deliverances’ if the plurality is to remain audible.
options.effect: Keeps the refuge image and potentially repeated acts of rescue; a literal plural can sound unusual.
options.held_by: ASV and WEB retain the stronghold with collective ‘salvation’; the Judaica Press translation preserves plural ‘salvations’.

options.choice: Express saving strength or the action of protecting and delivering.
options.effect: Makes the practical meaning clear and compact; reduces the fortress imagery and the plural form.
options.held_by: KJV uses ‘saving strength’; NET uses protective and delivering actions.

options.choice: Use Swete’s defender expression and identify its Greek basis.
options.effect: Links the defender wording with Greek verse 7; changes the Hebrew stronghold metaphor.
options.held_by: Swete 1896, Greek Psalm 27:8.

questions.question: How should the stronghold and plural deliverances be expressed?

questions.background: נַחֲלָתֶךָ is parallel to ‘your people’: the people themselves are God’s inheritance or possession, rather than people asking to receive an inheritance. Swete, Greek Psalm 27:9, retains κληρονομίαν. [NET note](https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Psa+28%3A8%2C9)

options.choice: Keep ‘your inheritance’ or ‘your heritage’.
options.effect: Preserves the traditional covenantal metaphor; listeners may misunderstand who inherits whom.
options.held_by: KJV, ASV, WEB and Swete; the Te Deum uses ‘heritage’.

options.choice: Identify the people as the nation or people who belong to God.
options.effect: Makes the relationship immediately clear; gives up the inheritance metaphor.
options.held_by: NET.

questions.question: Should the people remain God’s ‘inheritance’, or should their belonging to God be stated directly?

questions.background: וּרְעֵם asks God to shepherd them, encompassing tending, feeding and guiding. Swete, Greek Psalm 27:9, has ποίμανον, also a shepherding verb. The Te Deum’s governing language reflects a further interpretive and liturgical tradition.

options.choice: Retain ‘shepherd’ or ‘be their shepherd’.
options.effect: Keeps the pastoral metaphor and its range of care; requires the listener to infer its human application.
options.held_by: ASV and WEB; Swete’s Greek preserves the shepherding image.

options.choice: Emphasize feeding or tending.
options.effect: Makes provision or care explicit; foregrounds one part of the shepherd’s role.
options.held_by: KJV uses feeding; the Judaica Press translation uses tending.

options.choice: Use governing language and identify its liturgical interpretation.
options.effect: Connects with familiar Christian worship and royal guidance; removes the direct pastoral image.
options.held_by: Book of Common Prayer Te Deum.

questions.question: Which aspect of shepherding should the closing petition make audible?

questions.background: וְנַשְּׂאֵם comes from a verb that can mean lift, carry or exalt. Beside shepherding, carrying is a natural image; lifting or elevation is also represented in translation. Swete’s ἔπαρον, Greek Psalm 27:9, retains lifting language without expressly adding arms or shoulders.

options.choice: Express carrying or bearing the people up.
options.effect: Continues the shepherd’s care and support; chooses one sense of the broader lifting verb.
options.held_by: ASV and WEB.

options.choice: Keep ‘lift them up’ without specifying physical carrying or honor.
options.effect: Preserves useful ambiguity and traditional phrasing; may remain vague to listeners.
options.held_by: KJV and the Book of Common Prayer Te Deum; compatible with Swete’s lifting verb.

options.choice: Express elevation or exaltation.
options.effect: Makes restored standing or honor explicit; shifts attention away from pastoral carrying.
options.held_by: The Judaica Press translation displayed by Chabad.

questions.question: Should God be asked to carry the people, sustain them or raise them to honor?

questions.background: The wicked and neighbors have masculine grammatical forms that can refer to people generally. First-person speech does not itself identify the singer’s sex. God is addressed and referred to with masculine forms, and the anointed figure is grammatically singular masculine. English can retain divine pronouns or repeat the divine name without changing the human groups into males only.

options.choice: Use ungendered terms for human groups while retaining ‘he’ and ‘his’ for God and the anointed figure.
options.effect: Keeps the Hebrew reference structure while allowing any singer to voice the prayer; retains masculine divine language.
options.held_by: KJV, ASV and WEB broadly follow this pattern.

options.choice: Use ungendered human terms and repeat the divine name or ‘God’ where masculine divine pronouns can be avoided.
options.effect: Reduces masculine language for God; can lengthen phrases and alter pronoun-based connections.
options.held_by: The contemporary JPS rendering displayed by Sefaria uses this strategy in several lines. [Sefaria](https://www.sefaria.org/Psalms.28?with=Rashi)

questions.question: How should the setting distinguish generic human groups from masculine references to God and the anointed figure?

questions.background: בָּרוּךְ in verse 6 and וּבָרֵךְ in verse 9 share a root but function differently: the speaker acclaims God, then asks God to benefit the people. Swete also preserves related blessing words. English can preserve the lexical link or distinguish the actions explicitly.

options.choice: Keep ‘blessed’ or ‘bless’ in both places.
options.effect: Preserves the reciprocal verbal link and familiar worship language; leaves the difference in meaning to context.
options.held_by: KJV, ASV and WEB; Swete 1896, Greek Psalm 27:6 and 27:9.

options.choice: Use praise language for verse 6 and blessing or strengthening language for verse 9.
options.effect: Clarifies the different actions; loses the repeated Hebrew root.
options.held_by: NET distinguishes praise of the Lord from empowerment of the nation.

questions.question: Should the same English blessing word connect praise of God with the request for God’s blessing?
questions.topic: Blessing God and blessing the people

questions.background: עַד־הָעוֹלָם is an open-ended expression of lasting duration. Swete, Greek Psalm 27:9, has ἕως τοῦ αἰῶνος. ‘Forever’ is conventional; NET gives ‘at all times’ with ‘forever’ as an alternative. Neither wording by itself specifies resurrection or an afterlife.

options.choice: Close with ‘forever’ or an equivalent expression of unending duration.
options.effect: Gives an expansive, familiar final cadence; can encourage an explicitly eternal interpretation.
options.held_by: KJV, ASV and WEB.

options.choice: Close with ‘always’ or ‘at all times’.
options.effect: Emphasizes uninterrupted care; makes the far-reaching temporal horizon less explicit.
